_about: The fixed topic set Auto's style routing is checked against (TMDEV-203). expect: the right outcome(s), best first; ok: also acceptable; future: a coming style expected to take the topic over once its pack ships. Each style ticket updates these in its own merge. Read by tubematic_core/tests/test_style_routing.py and scripts/eval_style_routing.py. inserts_expect (TMDEV-224): the insert styles the insert step should choose for the picked main style, [] for none, or "any" (also when absent); inserts_ok: insert styles also acceptable.

cases.title: Ariane 5: A 64-Bit Number Squeezed Into 16 Bits
cases.brief: Why the first Ariane 5 rocket veered off course and was destroyed about 37 seconds after launch on 4 June 1996. One idea: guidance software reused from Ariane 4 converted a 64-bit floating-point value (the horizontal velocity bias) into a 16-bit signed integer. On Ariane 4 the number never got big enough to overflow; Ariane 5 was faster, the value overflowed, and the inertial reference computer shut down. The backup computer ran the same code and had already failed the same way 72 milliseconds earlier, so redundancy did not help. The main computer then read the error data as flight data and swung the nozzles hard over. Beats: the 16-bit box, the faster rocket, the overflow, the two identical failures, the change afterwards.
cases.note: Real-event probe, the brief as research writes it: one idea (a number conversion) and a beat list. The rocket is the subject; a number story it is not.

cases.title: Why the first Ariane 5 rocket destroyed itself
cases.brief: The first Ariane 5 veered off course and was blown up 37 seconds after launch on 4 June 1996. Guidance software reused from Ariane 4 could not hold the faster rocket's sideways speed, both guidance computers shut down, and the main computer steered on error data. Beats: the launch, the reused software, the shutdown, the hard turn, what changed afterwards.
cases.note: Real-event probe, plain wording: a real rocket, a real launch and a chain of causes inside it.

cases.title: The Mars probe lost to pounds and newtons
cases.brief: Why NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter burned up in 1999: one team's software reported thruster impulse in pound-seconds, the other read it as newton-seconds, a factor of 4.45. The small error added up over nine months and the probe arrived 170 km too low. Beats: the two teams, the number with no unit, the drift, the arrival, the fix.
cases.note: Real-event probe: a real spacecraft lost to a unit error. The arithmetic is one beat; the probe and its fate are the story.

Beats: the machine, the fast typist, the missing hardware interlock, the error message nobody understood, what changed.
cases.note: Real-event probe: a real machine and real overdoses caused by a software bug.

cases.title: The trading firm that lost $440 million in 45 minutes
cases.brief: How Knight Capital went under on 1 August 2012: a deployment missed one of eight servers, an old flag switched dead code back on, and that server bought high and sold low millions of times. Beats: the eight servers, the reused flag, the runaway orders, the 45 minutes, the bill.
cases.note: Real-event probe: a real company's failure told as an event, servers and all. System Flow can draw the servers but not the firm, the trading floor or the bill.

cases.title: Why Gangnam Style broke YouTube's view counter
cases.brief: In 2014 the video passed 2,147,483,647 views, the largest number a signed 32-bit integer can hold, and YouTube moved its counter to 64 bits. Beats: the counter, the 32-bit ceiling, what happens one past it, the fix, the new ceiling.
cases.note: Real-event pair probe, Photo Explainer vs Terminal Doc: a real video and its counter, but the number stays on screen, so Terminal Doc is acceptable.

cases.title: The Patriot missile that lost a third of a second
cases.brief: Why a Patriot battery in Dhahran failed to stop a Scud missile on 25 February 1991. One idea: the system counted time in tenths of a second, and 0.1 cannot be stored exactly in its 24-bit registers, so after 100 hours of running the clock had drifted 0.34 seconds and the radar looked in the wrong place. Beats: the battery, the tenth of a second, 100 hours of drift, the missed Scud, the patch that arrived a day later.
cases.note: Real-event probe with a number at its heart: the rounding error is one beat, the battery and the missed missile are the story.

cases.title: How one software bug blacked out 50 million people
cases.brief: The Northeast blackout of 14 August 2003: a race condition froze the alarm system at an Ohio utility, operators did not see sagging power lines hitting trees, and the failure cascaded across eight US states and Ontario in minutes. Beats: the control room, the silent alarm, the first line down, the cascade, the dark cities.
cases.note: Real-event probe: a real disaster whose cause is a software race. The cascade could be a diagram, but the cities, the control room and the scale need pictures.

cases.title: Why the Boeing 737 MAX kept pointing its nose down
cases.brief: How MCAS, flight software on the Boeing 737 MAX, read one faulty angle-of-attack sensor and pushed the nose down again and again, leading to the Lion Air and Ethiopian Airlines crashes in 2018 and 2019. Beats: the bigger engines, the single sensor, the repeated push, the pilots who did not know it existed, the grounding.
cases.note: Real-event probe: a real aircraft, real crashes and a software cause.

cases.title: The update that crashed 8.5 million Windows computers
cases.brief: The CrowdStrike outage of 19 July 2024: one faulty content update to a security sensor crashed Windows machines worldwide, grounding flights and taking banks and hospitals offline. Beats: the update, the blue screens, the airports and hospitals, the manual fix on every machine, the bill.
cases.note: Real-event probe: a real, recent outage with real places and screens to show.

cases.title: Why 2,147,483,647 is the biggest number in many programs
cases.brief: Where the number comes from: 31 bits of value and one sign bit, what happens when you add one to it, and why so many counters and timestamps are stored this way.
cases.note: Terminal Doc is an insert style: the string or the number is its insert, inside a main style that works the rest through. Negative control for the real-event rule: the same number as the Gangnam Style probe, with no real event. The number itself is the subject.

cases.title: How Heartbleed leaked server memory
cases.brief: The 2014 OpenSSL bug: a heartbeat message claims to carry 64 kilobytes but carries one byte, the server echoes back 64 kilobytes anyway, and the extra bytes are whatever sat next to it in memory: passwords, keys, cookies. Beats: the heartbeat, the lie about its length, the echo, what leaked, the one-line fix.
cases.note: System Flow is an insert style: the path between components is its insert, inside a main style that acts the parts out. Negative control for the real-failure rule: a real, named bug, but nothing to see beyond the requests and the bytes, so a diagram style stays right.

cases.title: Why Python's mutable default argument bites you
cases.brief: def add(item, items=[]): the empty list is made once, when the function is defined, so every call that leaves items out shares the same list. Show the code, the surprising output after two calls, and the fix with None.
cases.note: Insert probe (TMDEV-239/240): code being read, its output and its fix: Code Scenes.

cases.title: How an off-by-one error crashes a loop
cases.brief: A loop that runs one step too far reads past the end of a list: range(len(items) + 1), the IndexError it raises, and the one-character fix. Why the last index is one less than the length.
cases.note: Insert probe (TMDEV-239/240): a bug in a line of code and its fix: Code Scenes.

cases.title: How a missing bounds check becomes a buffer overflow
cases.brief: In C, strcpy copies a long name into a 16-byte buffer with no length check and writes over the memory next to it, including the return address. Show the code, what spills over and the bounded copy that fixes it.
cases.note: Insert probe (TMDEV-239/240): vulnerable code and its fix: Code Scenes; the memory layout may be a diagram.

cases.title: Why == is not is in Python
cases.brief: Two lists with the same items are equal (==) but not the same object (is). Show the two lines of code, what each comparison prints, and why small numbers seem to break the rule.
cases.note: Insert probe (TMDEV-239/240): pair with Terminal Doc: code being read and what it prints is Code Scenes, not a typed command.

cases.title: Why 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3 in your code
cases.brief: print(0.1 + 0.2) shows 0.30000000000000004: binary fractions cannot hold one tenth exactly. Show the line of code and its output, why the error appears, and how to compare money safely.
cases.note: Insert probe (TMDEV-239/240): a line of code and its output: Code Scenes; the long number alone could be Terminal Doc.

cases.title: What chmod 777 really does to a file
cases.brief: Typing chmod 777 on a file at the shell and running ls -l shows rwxrwxrwx: every user on the machine can read, change and run it. What each digit means and the safer 644.
cases.note: Insert probe (TMDEV-239/240): pair with Code Scenes: a command typed at a shell and its output is Terminal Doc.

cases.title: What curl -v shows about a web request
cases.brief: Run curl -v on a website and read what it prints: the address it connects to, the request lines it sends, the status code and headers that come back.
cases.note: Insert probe (TMDEV-239/240): pair with Code Scenes: a command at a shell and what it prints is Terminal Doc.

cases.title: The 'Hi Mum' text scam
cases.brief: A text from an unknown number says it is your child with a new phone, then asks you to pay a bill for them today. Read the messages one by one, mark the tells (the new number, the hurry, the money) and say what to do instead.
cases.note: Insert probe (TMDEV-239/240): messages exchanged in a scam: Format Packs.

cases.title: How a fake parcel-delivery text steals your card
cases.brief: A text says a parcel is held until you pay a small fee and links to a page that looks like a courier's. Read the message, point out the tells, and show what the fake page asks for.
cases.note: Insert probe (TMDEV-239/240): a scam text read message by message: Format Packs.

cases.title: The wrong-number text that turns into an investment scam
cases.brief: It starts with a polite text sent to the wrong number, becomes a friendly chat over weeks, and ends with a 'sure' crypto investment. Read the turning-point messages and the tells.
cases.note: Insert probe (TMDEV-239/240): a chat thread between people: Format Packs.

cases.title: Which of these passwords would you pick?
cases.brief: Put four passwords on the screen as a quiz (a long passphrase, a word with numbers, a short random string, a pet's name with a year) and ask which is strongest, then reveal why length wins.
cases.note: Insert probe (TMDEV-239/240): a which-is-true question; the main style (a board comparing the options) can carry it, so no insert is needed, and a Format Packs quiz or the passwords as Terminal Doc strings are both acceptable.

cases.title: Three signs a text from your bank is fake
cases.brief: Three tells, read in one breath: it asks you to tap a link, it says your account is locked, it wants a code sent to your phone. Then what your real bank never does.
cases.note: Insert probe (TMDEV-239/240): two to four numbered points: Format Packs list, or the scam text itself. Night Signal is acceptable: three rules against one fake sender.

cases.title: How the Great Fire of London spread
cases.brief: September 1666: a bakery fire on Pudding Lane, dry timber houses, an east wind, and four days that burned most of the city. Why it spread so fast and what changed after.
cases.note: Insert probe (TMDEV-239/240): negative control: no code, no messages. Archive and Engraving is acceptable too (TMDEV-230): an event from 1666 has no photographs, and period engravings are its real visual record.

cases.title: Why cats knock things off tables
cases.brief: Hunting instinct, attention and testing how things move: what researchers think is going on when a cat pushes a glass to the edge.
cases.note: Insert probe (TMDEV-239/240): negative control: no code, no messages.

cases.title: Why free cafe Wi-Fi can read your messages
cases.brief: A light, playful explainer: on an open cafe network anyone nearby can see what your laptop sends, a VPN or HTTPS seals it, and a few habits keep you safe. Beats: you at the cafe, the open network, the stranger reading along, the sealed tunnel, what to do next time.
cases.note: Paper Diorama: a privacy idea told as one familiar place with stand-in props (a note, a padlock) and a light narrator. Pair probe Paper Diorama vs Stick: no step-by-step mechanism with generic roles, so the room wins.

cases.title: What a password manager actually does
cases.brief: Your passwords as notes locked in one vault: one strong master key opens it, the vault fills in each login for you, and a stolen note from one site no longer opens the others. Told warmly, with a small joke about sticky notes on the monitor.
cases.note: Paper Diorama: a security idea told as a heist-proof vault with a before (sticky notes) and an after (the vault).

cases.title: How websites remember you with cookies
cases.brief: A playful explainer: a cookie is a little note the website hands your browser, which hands it back on every visit, like a diner that remembers your usual order. Beats: the first visit, the note, the next visit, the third-party note that follows you, clearing them.
cases.note: Paper Diorama: a web idea with an obvious familiar-place metaphor (a diner and an order slip) and a light register.

cases.title: Why two-factor login stops most account takeovers
cases.brief: A light explainer told as a vault with two locks: your password is one key, the code on your phone is the second, and a thief with only the first is left standing at the door. Beats: the stolen password, the second lock, the code arriving, the thief turned away, how to switch it on.
cases.note: Paper Diorama: a security fix told as a before and after in one familiar place (a vault), playful, with stand-in props.

cases.title: How a load balancer shares traffic between servers
cases.brief: Step by step: requests arrive at one front door, the balancer checks which servers are healthy, sends each request to the least busy one, and stops sending to a server that fails its health check.
cases.note: Pair probe Paper Diorama vs Stick: a process acted out step by step by generic roles stays with Stick Explainer, with a System Flow insert for the path.

cases.title: 5 phone settings to change for privacy today
cases.brief: A list of five separate settings, one each: location history, ad tracking, app permissions, lock-screen previews, Bluetooth scanning, and why each matters.
cases.note: Pair probe Paper Diorama vs Bean Explainer: a list of separate tips, one idea each, stays with Bean Explainer even when the subject is privacy.

cases.title: How the Sun took the Earth's place at the centre of everything
cases.brief: How an old belief was overturned: the Earth-centred heavens of Ptolemy, Copernicus's quiet book in 1543, Galileo's telescope and his trial in 1633, and how the new picture finally won. Told gravely, as a history of an idea passed from one thinker to the next.
cases.note: Archive and Engraving: an old belief overturned by a new one, with dated thinkers as name cards and engraved plates. Pair probe Archive vs Storybook Atlas: a grave history of an idea, not a playful origin story.

cases.title: Why sailors could not find their longitude for two hundred years
cases.brief: The longitude problem: ships lost because no one could tell how far east or west they were, the 1714 prize, the clockmakers and astronomers who competed for it, and the sea clock that finally solved it. Old charts, routes and machines.
cases.note: Archive and Engraving: voyages and routes on old charts, a dated rivalry, engraved machines.

cases.title: How tulips caused history's first famous market bubble
cases.brief: Amsterdam in the 1630s: tulip bulbs traded on paper contracts, prices climbing past the cost of a house, and the crash of February 1637. What the records say happened, and what later tellings exaggerated.
cases.note: Archive and Engraving: economic history told through dates, documents and engraved scenes, in a documentary register.

cases.title: The doctor who told other doctors to wash their hands
cases.brief: Vienna, 1847: Ignaz Semmelweis noticed that mothers died far more often in the ward run by doctors than in the one run by midwives, ordered hand-washing in chlorine, and was ignored and mocked. How an idea that saves lives was refused for decades.
cases.note: Archive and Engraving: an overturned belief, a dated biography told through work and places, a grave subject. The person is a name card, never a portrait.

cases.title: Where the word robot came from
cases.brief: A playful origin story: a 1920 Czech play, the playwright's brother who suggested the word, what it first meant, and how it spread into science fiction and factories.
cases.note: Pair probe Archive vs Storybook Atlas: the light origin story of an everyday word stays with Storybook Atlas.

cases.title: What Pompeii looked like the day Vesuvius erupted
cases.brief: The town, its streets and houses as they were in AD 79, the eruption hour by hour, and what the excavations found under the ash.
cases.note: Pair probe Archive vs Photo Explainer: a real place the viewer came to see in full-frame pictures stays with Photo Explainer, however old the event.

cases.title: The spreadsheet error behind a decade of austerity
cases.brief: In 2010 an economics paper said debt above 90% of GDP slows growth; governments quoted it to justify cuts. In 2013 a student found a spreadsheet error that left out countries. Told as an investigation: the paper, who cited it, the student's check, the corrected numbers, what changed.
cases.note: Editorial Collage: a real story told through documents, dates, quotes and numbers, with nothing physical to photograph. Pair probe Editorial Collage vs Photo Explainer: no real object to show, so the evidence desk wins.

cases.title: How the Equifax breach unfolded, day by day
cases.brief: 2017: an unpatched web server, attackers inside for 76 days, 147 million people's records taken, a delayed announcement, executives' share sales, the fines. Traced as a timeline of dates, memos and numbers across the company, the regulators and the public.
cases.note: Editorial Collage: a named breach told as a timeline of documents and numbers spreading across firms and people. Photo Explainer is acceptable for the real company.

cases.title: Why the 2010 Flash Crash wiped a trillion dollars in 36 minutes
cases.brief: 6 May 2010: one large sell order, high-speed traders passing contracts back and forth, prices of some shares falling to a cent, a market that recovered within the hour, and the five-year hunt that ended at a trader in his parents' house. Dates, figures and the investigation.
cases.note: Editorial Collage: a market event told through figures, timestamps and an investigation's findings.

cases.title: How one leaked password shut down America's largest fuel pipeline
cases.brief: May 2021, Colonial Pipeline: an old VPN account with no second factor, a ransomware gang, a pipeline shut for six days, queues at petrol stations, a ransom paid and partly recovered. Told cause by cause through the dates, the notes and the numbers.
cases.note: Editorial Collage: a named incident traced cause by cause across a company, its customers and the government, told as an evidence board.

cases.title: What the Chernobyl reactor looked like after the explosion
cases.brief: The reactor building, the control room and the town of Pripyat as they looked after 26 April 1986, and what the pictures show about what went wrong.
cases.note: Pair probe Editorial Collage vs Photo Explainer: real places the viewer came to see as full-frame pictures stay with Photo Explainer.

cases.title: How a fake invoice tricks a company into paying a stranger
cases.brief: Told as a story the viewer steps into: you run accounts payable, an email from a known supplier says their bank details changed, the invoice looks right, you pay, the real supplier calls. What the scam is called and how it is caught.
cases.note: Pair probe Editorial Collage vs Case File Story: an invented second-person scheme ending on a choice stays with Case File Story.

cases.title: The boy who cried wolf, and what it teaches about trust
cases.brief: Retell the fable of the shepherd boy who raised false alarms until nobody came when the wolf was real, as a calm story, and end on the lesson for today: trust is spent each time we cry wolf.
cases.note: Storybook Reveal: a fable with one protagonist retold as a lesson.

cases.title: The tortoise and the hare, and why slow and steady still wins
cases.brief: The old race between a boastful hare and a patient tortoise, told page by page as a bedtime story, ending on what it means for anyone tempted to rush.
cases.note: Storybook Reveal: a moral tale, warm and calm.

cases.title: How one page a day turned a girl into a reader
cases.brief: A small story about an invented girl who reads one page every night before bed, and how the habit quietly grows until she has read a whole shelf. Told as a gentle tale about how small habits compound.
cases.note: Storybook Reveal: a habit told through one character's small story. Pair probe vs Bean Explainer: one story, not a list of tips.

cases.title: The fisherman who already had enough
cases.brief: The parable of a rich visitor who tells a happy village fisherman to work harder, buy boats and retire one day to fish in peace, which is what the fisherman already does. A calm tale about contentment.
cases.note: Storybook Reveal: a parable with a lesson, one protagonist, no facts or figures.

cases.title: How the teddy bear got its name
cases.brief: A light origin story: a 1902 hunting trip, a president who refused to shoot a tied bear, a newspaper cartoon, and the toymakers who named a stuffed bear after him.
cases.note: Pair probe Storybook Reveal vs Storybook Atlas: real history with a named person stays with Storybook Atlas; a told tale cannot show a real person.

cases.title: A week in the life of a remote worker who never takes a break
cases.brief: Follow Sam, a remote worker, from Monday to Friday: the laptop at breakfast, the skipped lunch, the late calls, the colleague who notices, and the small changes Sam makes. Everyday scenes with recurring characters.
cases.note: Pair probe Storybook Reveal vs Illustrated: recurring characters in an everyday modern story told in scenes stay with Illustrated.

cases.title: Five ways to stop putting things off
cases.brief: A quick list of tricks against procrastination: the two-minute rule, breaking a task into tiny steps, a timer, removing the phone, and a reward at the end. One tip each.
cases.note: Pair probe Storybook Reveal vs Bean Explainer: a list of tips, one idea each, stays with Bean Explainer even when the subject is a habit.

cases.title: How to turn on two-factor login
cases.brief: Step by step: open your account's security settings, choose an authenticator app, scan the QR code, type the six-digit code, save the backup codes. Why a stolen password is then not enough.
cases.note: A numbered procedure a viewer follows on their own phone: Mid-century How-To. Bean Explainer is for a list of named items with no order to follow.

cases.title: Back up your phone in three steps
cases.brief: How to make sure your photos survive a lost or broken phone: turn on cloud backup in settings, plug in on wifi overnight, then check the date of the last backup.
cases.note: A short procedure with a done state at the end.

cases.title: Set up a password manager in four steps
cases.brief: Install a password manager, make one strong master password, import the passwords saved in your browser, then turn on autofill so you never type one again.
cases.note: Setting something up from start to done.

cases.title: What to do when a pan catches fire
cases.brief: The safe steps when cooking oil catches fire: turn off the heat, slide a lid over the pan, never pour water on it, and leave it covered until it cools. Why water makes it explode.
cases.note: A safety rule told as steps to follow, the 1950s safety-film register.

cases.title: Check a link before you click it
cases.brief: How to spot a fake link in a message: hold your finger on it to see the real address, read the domain from right to left, look for swapped letters, and open the site yourself instead.
cases.note: Pair probe with Bean Explainer's scam lists: these are steps a viewer does in order, not a catalogue of tricks.

cases.title: Five password mistakes everyone makes
cases.brief: Reusing one password everywhere, using your pet's name, adding 1 at the end, writing it on a sticky note, and never turning on two-factor login: each mistake and why it gets you hacked.
cases.note: Pair probe with Mid-century How-To: a list of named mistakes, one section each, is Bean Explainer's even though the topic is security advice.

cases.title: How eight bits make a byte
cases.brief: Why computers count in bits, how eight of them make a byte, why a byte holds 256 patterns, and how one byte stores the letter A.
cases.note: Units that add up, drawn as cubes that join: Process Cast. Whiteboard is acceptable for the arithmetic.

cases.title: How your white blood cells catch a virus
cases.brief: A virus gets into your body; the cells that patrol your blood spot it, call for help, copy themselves and swallow it, and remember it for next time.
cases.note: Cells as the characters of a process inside the body.

cases.title: Meet the seven layers of the OSI model
cases.brief: The seven layers of networking introduced one by one, from the cable up to the app, each with the one job it does for a message passing through.
cases.note: Pair probe with Bean Explainer's lists: named parts of a system introduced one by one as characters is Process Cast's meet-the-cast.

cases.title: What a compiler does to your code, stage by stage
cases.brief: Your source code goes through the lexer, the parser, the type checker, the optimiser and the code generator, and each stage hands the next a different version of it.
cases.note: A pipeline of named stages each part passes through.

cases.title: What happens to a sandwich after you swallow it
cases.brief: The trip through your stomach, small intestine and liver: what each organ does to the food, which parts become energy, and what is left over.
cases.note: Organs and food as characters at stations along one path.

cases.title: How a phishing attacker steals your login
cases.brief: An attacker sends a fake email, you click the link, a copy of your bank's page takes your password, and the attacker logs in as you before you notice.
cases.note: Pair probe with Process Cast: the actors are people and roles (an attacker and a user), which is Stick Explainer's.

cases.title: Antibiotics vs superbugs: the arms race
cases.brief: Round one, a new antibiotic knocks the bacteria out. A few survivors carry a gene that resists it; they multiply, and the next drug has to hit harder. Who is winning now, and what keeps the drugs working.
cases.note: Two sides fighting round by round, a move and an answer: Comic Panels.

cases.title: Your password vs a guessing attack
cases.brief: Round one, the attacker tries the hundred most common passwords. Round two, a whole dictionary. Round three, every combination. How each extra character holds the attack off for years longer.
cases.note: A defender against an invader, told as a showdown. Whiteboard is acceptable for the arithmetic of the guesses.

cases.title: Spam filter vs spammer: the endless fight
cases.brief: Spammers misspell words, hide text in pictures and rent fresh addresses; each time, the filter learns the trick and blocks it, and the spammer comes back with a new one.
cases.note: An arms race told move by move between a hero and a villain.

cases.title: Captain Patch and the zero-day villain
cases.brief: A short comic about Captain Patch, an invented hero who guards a city's computers, and the villain who slips in through a hole nobody knew about, until Patch closes it.
cases.note: Pair probe, Comic Panels vs Illustrated: an invented hero, but a villain and a fight, told in balloons and sound effects.

cases.title: How a firewall decides what gets in
cases.brief: Every packet that reaches your network is checked against a list of rules: where it comes from, which port it wants, and whether it belongs to a connection you started.
cases.note: Pair probe with Comic Panels: a defender, but no fight told round by round; a mechanism walked through by roles, which is Stick Explainer's.

cases.title: You're a Roman legionary for twenty-five years
cases.brief: You sign up at seventeen: the pay is docked for your own gear, you march twenty miles a day into Gaul, and twenty-five years later you retire with a small farm.
cases.note: Second-person history: a job and its rules in a past era, with a contract, a map and a reversal at the end.

cases.title: A week as a medieval peasant
cases.brief: You farm the lord's land three days a week for free, hand a tenth of your harvest to the church, pay to grind your grain at his mill, and still owe rent.
cases.note: Daily life and work in a past era told to 'you', the rules stacking up against you: Puppet History. Cartoon 3D is acceptable for the place.

cases.title: Why the US bought Alaska for two cents an acre
cases.brief: In 1867 Russia sells Alaska to the United States for 7.2 million dollars; newspapers mock it as Seward's Folly, until gold is found thirty years later.
cases.note: Why a historical event happened, with a map, a price on a contract and a reversal; the real people appear only by name. Pair probe with Archive and Engraving: told as a serious documentary on old maps and newspapers, that style fits too.

cases.title: Life in the trenches of World War One
cases.brief: What a soldier's day in a Western Front trench was like in 1916: the mud, the rats, the rotation between the front line and reserve, and the shelling.
cases.note: Pair probe with Puppet History: a past-era daily life, but a war's suffering is a tragedy, which that style never plays for laughs. Told through pictures of the real place: Photo Explainer.

cases.title: If a stranger sends you a QR code, don't scan it
cases.brief: A second-person warning: a stranger messages you a QR code that looks like a parking ticket. Rule one: don't scan it. Why: the code hides where the link goes. What to do instead: preview the link, check the address, pay in the real app.
cases.note: A deadpan rule against one threat, told to you: Night Signal. Pair probe with Case File Story: no money story and no choice at the end.

cases.title: What to do in the first hour after your phone is stolen
cases.brief: Your phone is gone at 2 a.m. Four steps in the right order: lock it remotely, call your carrier before anyone swaps the SIM, change the email password from another device, warn your bank.
cases.note: Safety steps for a bad moment, numbered, second person: Night Signal.

cases.title: Never answer these three kinds of calls
cases.brief: Three rules for calls that are traps: the missed call from an unknown country code, the 'is this you?' silence, the bank that asks you to read back a code. Each rule, why, and what to do instead.
cases.note: Numbered rules, each against one threat: Night Signal. Pair probe with Bean Explainer, which takes a looser list of tips.

cases.title: If someone knocks at 3 a.m. saying they are from the gas company
cases.brief: A creepy hypothetical told as a case: the knock, the doorbell camera, the uniform that looks almost right. Rule: never open the door, call the company's real number, and here is why the hour gives it away.
cases.note: A stranger at the door, a camera and one threat: Night Signal.

cases.title: A stranger asks you to cash a cheque for them
cases.brief: You are at the bank machine when a polite stranger asks you to deposit their cheque and hand them the cash. Follow what happens over the next week when the cheque bounces, and end on what you would do.
cases.note: Pair probe for Night Signal: a scheme told as a story with you inside it, the money moving and a choice at the end, is Case File Story; Night Signal (a warning with a red threat) is acceptable.

cases.title: How deep the ocean really goes
cases.brief: From the surface to the bottom of the Mariana Trench: where divers stop, where sperm whales hunt, where the Titanic lies, and the 10,900 metres to the bottom, with something familiar for scale at each depth.
cases.note: Depths with units, creatures and a descent: Flat Vector Science. Pair probe with Photo Explainer, which takes real named things seen as pictures.

cases.title: How big the biggest known star is
cases.brief: Start with the Earth, then the Sun, then bigger and bigger stars until the largest known one, which would swallow the orbit of Jupiter. Each step compared with the last.
cases.note: A ladder of sizes in space: Flat Vector Science. Whiteboard would only fit if the sizes were worked out as arithmetic.

cases.title: What happens to your body at the bottom of the ocean
cases.brief: The pressure at 11 kilometres down, what it does to air in your lungs, to your ears, to a submarine hull, with the numbers in atmospheres and a bus-on-your-thumb comparison.
cases.note: What would happen to you in nature, told with numbers and a depth: Flat Vector Science. Pair probe with Bean Explainer, which takes everyday body topics told as a list.

cases.title: How a virus copies itself inside a cell
cases.brief: A virus latches onto a cell, slips inside, hijacks the machinery to build copies of itself, and bursts out: four stages, with how many copies one virus makes.
cases.note: A natural process in stages with a cell and a virus as the subjects: Flat Vector Science. Pair probe with Stick Explainer, which takes processes acted out by roles.

cases.title: How many Earths fit inside the Sun
cases.brief: Work it out: the Sun's radius is 109 Earth radii, so its volume is 109 cubed, about 1.3 million Earths. Show the multiplication step by step.
cases.note: Pair probe for Flat Vector Science: a quantity worked out as arithmetic is Whiteboard, even when the subject is space; Flat Vector Science is acceptable.

cases.title: How a parcel gets from the warehouse to your door
cases.brief: Follow one parcel: the shelf in a warehouse outside the city, the truck to the sorting depot, the belts that sort it, the van for your street, and the 36 hours it takes in all.
cases.note: One item's physical journey through a system of places, with a running count: Isometric Infographic. Pair probe with Stick Explainer, which takes a process acted out by people as roles.

cases.title: How water gets from the reservoir to your tap
